compiler_and_flags: C++23 (GCC 13+/Clang 17+/MSVC per README); README states the C++ core is built in Release mode with -O3 for the Go/OCI benchmark; exact compiler and version for the CLI table not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon W-2235 host; Ubuntu 22.04 WSL2 guest exposing 5 cores / 10 logical CPUs; median of 7 timed samples after 1 warm-up; raw samples archived in benchmarks/results/2026-07-14/report-benchmarks.json
name: pigzpp
workload: Compress a 128 MB multilingual (English + Chinese Wikipedia) text corpus at level 6 with 8 workers on the command line; also decompression of a level-6 gzip stream.
claimed_speedup: CLI compress: gzip 1.12 -6 17 MB/s (ratio 2.83); pigz 2.6 -6 -p8 133 MB/s (2.83); pigzpp --engine zlib 285 MB/s (2.81), stated as 2.1x faster than pigz at the same ratio; pigzpp --engine isal (default) 1124 MB/s (2.58), stated as 8.5x faster than pigz with about 9% more output. Decompression: pigzpp 711 MB/s vs pigz 212 MB/s vs gzip 166 MB/s.
tradeoffs: Library plus CLI with C API, Python, Go, Rust and WASM bindings; speed comes from the zlib-ng and ISA-L DEFLATE backends. ISA-L backend is x86-64 only and gives about 9% larger output (ratio 2.58 vs 2.81); on ARM64 and WASM only the zlib-ng path is available.
caveats: Very new, single-author C++23 rewrite of pigz. Baseline pigz uses the system zlib, so much of the gain is zlib-ng and ISA-L (both already catalogued) rather than new compression code. Benchmarks ran in a WSL2 guest, one CPU, one text corpus. The 8.5x figure trades ratio. An arXiv paper (2608.24153) appeared in search results but arXiv is blocked here; numbers were read from the README only. Exact compiler name/version for the CLI run not stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pigzpp: Fast, Parallel, Portable Compression for the Whole Stack github' (led from a search on QPL/deflate comparisons)

name: Snappy
workload: Compress and decompress a benchmark suite of text, HTML and binary files on one core, compared with zlib in its fastest mode.
claimed_speedup: README: compared to the fastest mode of zlib, Snappy is an order of magnitude faster for most inputs, with compressed files 20% to 100% bigger. Single core of a Core i7 in 64-bit mode: compresses at about 250 MB/sec or more and decompresses at about 500 MB/sec or more (slowest inputs in the suite). Typical ratios 1.5-1.7x plain text vs 2.6-2.8x for zlib fastest mode.
stars_or_usage: 6.6k stars; used in production at Google
tradeoffs: Much lower compression ratio than zlib (files 20-100% larger). Optimized for 64-bit little-endian x86 with cheap unaligned loads; may run slower elsewhere.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no exact CPU, compiler, flags or zlib version; the speed claim is qualitative ('order of magnitude'). Modern LZ4 and zstd fast modes match or beat Snappy, so this is a historical win over zlib, not over today's fast codecs. Repo includes snappy_test_tool that benchmarks against zlib, LZO, LZF and QuickLZ when installed.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github C++ compression library faster than zlib benchmark lzbench density miniz snappy zstd lz4 comparison'

name: FastLZ
workload: Compress and decompress enwik8 (100 MB text), compared with zlib levels 1 and 9 (via lzbench per the README).
claimed_speedup: enwik8: FastLZ ratio 54.2%, 159 MB/s compress, 305 MB/s decompress; zlib -1 ratio 42.3%, 50 MB/s, 184 MB/s; zlib -9 ratio 36.5%, 11 MB/s, 185 MB/s. (ratio is compressed size as percent of input, so FastLZ output is larger.)
stars_or_usage: 544 stars; used in Godot, HHVM, Apache Traffic Server, Netty, Death Stranding per README
tradeoffs: Byte-aligned LZ77 with worse ratio than zlib (54.2% vs 42.3% at level 1). ANSI C/C90, small and portable; bindings for Rust, Python, JS, Ruby, Lua.
caveats: README table has no CPU, compiler, flags or lzbench version; numbers appear to be from an old lzbench run. LZ4 and Snappy are generally faster than FastLZ today.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github C++ compression library faster than zlib benchmark lzbench density miniz snappy zstd lz4 comparison' (README read from FastLZ repo)

name: LZHAM (lzham_codec_devel)
workload: Matt Mahoney's 10GB benchmark, 7-Zip with LZHAM plugin vs LZMA at -mx=9 with 64 MB dictionary, archive test (decompression) time.
claimed_speedup: README: ratio similar to LZMA with 1.5x-8x faster decompression. 10GB benchmark: LZHAM -mx=9 3,573,782,721 bytes, archive test time 71.292 s; LZMA -mx=9 3,560,052,414 bytes, 223.050 s (about 3.1x faster test time, derived from page data); LZHAM -mx=8 3,577,047,629 bytes, 70.652 s.
stars_or_usage: 82 stars; 7-Zip plugin; used in game asset pipelines
tradeoffs: Very slow, offline-oriented compressor. Decompression is slower than zlib and has a higher init cost than LZMA, so LZMA wins for inputs below roughly 1000-13000 bytes per README. C++03.
caveats: Results are the author's own run on a 32-bit 7-Zip plugin build; CPU, compiler and flags not stated. Repo is the 'unstable/experimental' v1.1 devel branch; stable v1.0 lives in a separate repo. README says public domain while the repo shows MIT. Test time includes disk and archive overhead rather than pure decode.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github C++ compression library faster than zlib benchmark lzbench ...' then compression README sweep (candidate list from LZMA/xz alternatives)

hardware: 3GHz quad-core Intel Core2, 8GB RAM, SSD, lrzip v0.612 (first table); 2.53GHz dual-core Core2, 4GB, lrzip v0.5.1 (second table)
name: lrzip
baseline: xz and 7z (LZMA), plus bzip2 and gzip
workload: Compress a Linux 2.6.37 kernel tarball (430,612,480 bytes) with default options; also six consecutive kernel trees (2.37 GB).
tradeoffs: Needs large RAM for long-range dedup window; wins mainly on large files with distant redundancy (hundreds of MB apart). Multithreaded across blocks, so wall-clock gains come partly from using 4 cores against single-threaded xz.
caveats: Old (Core2-era) numbers on one doc file, no compiler or flags, xz and 7z of that era single-threaded. Comparison is wall time with lrzip using all cores. Modern multithreaded xz (-T) and zstd --long would narrow or reverse the gap. Author's own benchmark.
found_via: GitHub page README of ckolivas/lrzip, surfaced while sweeping LZMA/xz alternatives

compiler_and_flags: Rust >= 1.85; Cargo.toml release profile lto="fat", codegen-units=1, opt-level default (3); Criterion harness; liblz4 build flags not confirmed
hardware: Intel Xeon 8481C, AMD EPYC 9B14, AWS Neoverse V2 (ARM), Apple M2 Max (separate run)
name: lzvolt
language: Rust (hand-written assembly decoders; C header and cdylib/staticlib callable from C++)
workload: Decode throughput on small values (records and varied data of 512 B, 4 KiB, 64 KiB, plus incompressible noise), codec vs liblz4 on its own format, same bytes and process, medians of three runs on three machines.
claimed_speedup: Decoding own format, GiB/s and margin over liblz4: varied 64 KiB 7.01 (+72%) Xeon 8481C, 8.40 (+64%) EPYC 9B14, 8.15 (+83%) Neoverse V2; records 512 B 9.44 (+29%), 10.78 (+33%), 10.60 (+22%); 18 of 18 cells +14% to +83%. Reading raw LZ4 blocks: ahead on 20 of 27 cells. Packing: ahead on 25 of 27 and smaller output.
tradeoffs: Own format is not LZ4-compatible (also reads LZ4 blocks). Encoder refuses data it cannot shrink by an eighth. Targets small values for caches and record stores, not large-file streaming. Per-CPU hand-written assembly; C API (include/lzvolt.h) is the only supported path from C++.
caveats: Brand-new single-author project with 0 stars; latest commit (2026-10-02) was 'Correct a misattributed benchmark table in the README', so verifiers should re-read the current tables. Throughput counted against unpacked bytes, so smaller output inflates the number. Loses 12-15% on x86 on 512-byte noise in LZ4 format (author states this). The implementation language is Rust, usable from C++ only through its C ABI. Measures only against liblz4, not zstd.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github fast LZ77 compressor SIMD "faster than" zstd lz4 decompression speed C++ new 2025'

name: Inflate++ (inflatecpp)
workload: Decompress a 60,132,846-byte zlib stream (large raw texture) and a 147,120,395-byte gzip archive; time in microseconds.
claimed_speedup: zlib bitstream: zlib inflate 1.2.11 134,245 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 118,399 us (91%); without checksum 110,238 us (85%). gzip bitstream: zlib 465,567 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 362,133 us (87%); without checksum 265,462 us (65%). (About 1.1-1.15x faster with checksum, derived from page data.)
tradeoffs: Single-call, memory-to-memory decompressor under 1000 lines of C++ plus about 250 lines of Adler-32; no streaming API mentioned.
caveats: No CPU, compiler or flags; two inputs only; the 'without checksum' rows skip verification that zlib performs, so they are not like-for-like. Baseline zlib 1.2.11 is old and zlib-ng and libdeflate are far faster than both.

name: memlz
baseline: LZ4 (with acceleration around 32 to 64), Snappy, FastLZ, LZO
workload: Single-thread compression of enwik8, Silesia and employees_50MB.json on an Intel i7 with non-cached memcpy speed of 14000 MB/s.
claimed_speedup: README: 'world's fastest compression library, running at 5 - 7 GB/s in one thread'; Snappy, FastLZ and LZO have better ratios but compression speeds well below 1000 MB/s; only LZ4 with acceleration set around 32 to 64 comes close. Per-codec numbers appear only in linked PNG figures, not in text. Decompression 'less competitive depending on the data type'.
tradeoffs: Header-only C/C++, streaming mode with no extra memcpy, bounds-safe decompression. Trades ratio for compress speed and the format may change (README marks it beta).
caveats: Numbers live in images I could not read; text claim is qualitative apart from the 5-7 GB/s figure. README says memlz was added to lzbench and TurboBench, but I did not open those results. Compares only against LZ4 at an extreme acceleration setting. Beta, compatibility may break.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github open-source compressor "faster than zstd" OR "faster than brotli" same ratio C++ library lzbench enwik8 silesia benchmark 2026'

name: Stenos
baseline: Blosc + Zstd (shuffle then Zstd) and LZ4
workload: Compress structured binary arrays (integers, floats) from the stenos_dataset; plots compression ratio versus speed against Blosc with byte or bit shuffle plus Zstd, single thread.
claimed_speedup: README: 'usually compress better and faster than Blosc + Zstd or lz4'; SIMD block algorithm compresses at 'more or less 2GB/s and decompress at 3GB/s'. Comparison data is in docs/benchmarks.svg only, no numeric table in text.
tradeoffs: For arrays of fixed-width numeric elements, not general byte streams; depends on Zstd; SIMD block mode needs SSE4.1/AVX2 and is skipped on ARM; no streaming compression yet.
caveats: Baseline is Blosc+Zstd, not plain zstd, and the comparison is a graph I could not read numerically. Own benchmark and dataset; compiler and flags not stated. Not a general-purpose byte compressor.

hardware: AMD Ryzen 3900X (12 cores / 24 threads) per pigzbench; neurolabusc/pigz-bench uses a 24-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8260
name: pigz
workload: Third-party zlib-ng/pigzbench: Silesia corpus (and NIfTI brain imaging data), 12-core AMD Ryzen 3900X, comparing pigz built with system zlib, Cloudflare zlib and zlib-ng against gzip, pbzip2 and zstd.
claimed_speedup: pigzbench decompression table (Speed MB/s): pigz-CF 307, pigz-ng 361, pigz-Sys 306, gzip 189, pbzip2 448, zstd 528. Compression results are only in PNG graphs (silesia_speed_threads.png, silesia_speed_size.png) that I could not read.
tradeoffs: Parallel gzip using multiple cores; output is standard gzip but block boundaries cost a little ratio; decompression is only partly parallel; needs zlib 1.2.3+ and pthreads.
caveats: Maintenance flag is 'abandoned' only by the 3-year commit rule; v2.8 (Aug 2022) is the stable release. pigzbench does not state compiler flags and its compression numbers are in graphs. Gains over gzip come from using more cores, not a faster single-thread algorithm. The pigzbench page row was read through a page summary tool; verify against the page. This pigz entry uses the zlib-ng organization's benchmark repo as evidence.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github parallel gzip OR xz OR zstd compressor multithreaded faster than pigz xz benchmark C++' (pigzbench), then github.com/madler/pigz
